Allah's words ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾

In the thing sworn by there is the glorification of the Qur'an and its description as "full of reminder," which includes a reminder to the servants of what they need, and nobility and worth that point to the thing sworn to: that it is the truth from Allah, not fabricated, as the disbelievers say.

This is the meaning of the statement of many of the exegetes, earlier and later, that the answer (jawab) to the oath is omitted, its implied sense being: "Indeed the Qur'an is true."

This is consistent in every case of this kind.

As for the statement of some that the answer is Allah's words ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾, interposed between the oath and its answer by His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾, it is far-fetched, because kam (how many) is not preceded by an oath. You do not say "By Allah, how much wealth I spent" or "By Allah, how many slaves I freed."

Those who held this view, since this was not hidden from them, felt the need to posit something that the answer could be attached to, namely "Indeed, We destroyed [them]."

Even more distant is the view of the one who says the answer is in Allah's words ﴿Indeed, all but the messengers did not [do anything] except deny﴾.

More distant still is the view of the one who says the answer is ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾.

More distant still is the view of the one who says the answer is Allah's words ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾.

The closest thing said regarding the answer in wording, though distant in meaning, is that narrated from Qatadah and others: that it is in His words ﴿But those who disbelieve﴾.

As in His words ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an. But they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾.

The author of al-Nazm (Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm) explained this view, saying: the meaning of "bal" (but/rather) is to emphasize the statement that follows it, so it becomes like the emphatic "inna" in affirming what follows it.

It was said that here it is in the position of "inna," because it emphasizes what follows it of the statement, though it has another meaning, namely negating a previous statement. So it is as if He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "Ṣād. By the Qur'an full of reminder, indeed those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition."

Just as you say: "By Allah, indeed Zayd is standing."

He said: the proponent of this view argued that although this arrangement has no basis in Arabic and no precedent in its usage, it may be an arrangement that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created, given the possibility we have mentioned that "bal" may carry the meaning of "inna." End.

Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians say that "bal" may occur in the answer to an oath just as "inna" does, because its purpose is to emphasize the statement.

This view is the preference of Abu Hatim, and al-Akhfash related it from the Kufans.

Some of them established it by saying: the original sentence is ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ and ﴿By the Qur'an full of reminder﴾; then when the oath was placed first, it was left in its state.

Al-Akhfash said: this is what the Kufans say, and it is not good in Arabic. If you say "By Allah, he stood" meaning "he stood, by Allah," it is not good.

Al-Nahhas said: this is an error according to the grammarians, because when one begins with the oath and the speech depends on it, there must be an answer.

They agreed that it is not permissible to say "By Allah, Amr stood" meaning "Amr stood, by Allah," because the speech relies on the oath.

Al-Akhfash mentioned another aspect regarding the answer to the oath, saying: it is permissible that "Ṣād" has a meaning on which the oath falls, which we do not know, as if he were saying "the truth, by Allah."

Abu al-Hasan al-Wahidi said: what al-Akhfash said is correct in meaning according to the view of those who say "Ṣād" means "the truthful one is Allah" or "Muhammad has spoken the truth."

Al-Farra' also mentioned this aspect, saying: "Ṣād" is the answer to the oath, and he said it is like your saying "it is obligatory, by Allah" and "he left, by Allah," so it is the answer to His words ﴿and the Qur'an﴾.

Al-Nahhas and others mentioned another aspect regarding the answer: that it is omitted, its implied sense being: "And by the Qur'an full of reminder, the matter is as these disbelievers say," and what indicates the omitted part is His words ﴿But those who disbelieve﴾.

This is the preference of Ibn Jarir, and it is derived from the statement of Qatadah. Al-Jurjani explained it, saying: "bal" both retracts a statement before it and affirms a statement after it. The preceding and following are evident, and the evident indicates the hidden. So when this is the case, His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ must be contrary to this implied meaning, as if it were said: "By the Qur'an full of reminder, indeed those who disbelieve claim that they are upon the truth," or whatever has this meaning.

So these are six aspects, apart from what we began with regarding the answer to the oath. And Allah knows best.

(A subtle point)

Consider the surahs that begin with single letters: how you find the surah built upon the words of that letter. Among them is (Qaf), and the surah is built upon words containing the letter qaf: mention of the Qur'an, mention of creation, repetition of speech and its returning again and again, nearness to the son of Adam, the two angels receiving the servant's speech, mention of the Watcher, mention of the driver and the companion, being cast into Hell, the advance of threat, mention of the pious, mention of the heart, the generations, and the search through the lands, mention of "qawl" (speech) twice, the cleaving of the earth and the casting of firm mountains into it, the towering palm trees and provision, mention of a people, and the realization of the threat.

Even if there were nothing but the repetition of speech and dialogue, there is another secret: that all the meanings of this surah are suited to what is in the letter qaf of intensity, loudness, height and openness.

If you wish further clarification of this, consider what the surah of (Ṣād) contains of multiple disputes: first, the dispute of the disbelievers with the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ up to the end of their speech; then the dispute of the two litigants before David; then the disputing of the people of the Fire; then the Highest Assembly disputed about knowledge, which is the degrees and expiations; then the disputing of Iblis and his objection to his Lord regarding His command to prostrate to Adam; then his dispute a second time concerning his descendants, his oath to mislead them all except the sincere among them.

Let the intelligent and discerning consider whether anything other than (Ṣād) befits this surah, and whether anything other than the letter qaf befits the surah of (Qaf). This is a drop from the ocean of some of the secrets of these letters. And Allah knows best.

(Section: On the difference between the patience of the noble and the patience of the base)

Everyone must bear some of what they dislike, either by choice or by compulsion.

The noble person bears by choice, knowing the good outcome of patience, that he will be praised for it and blamed for impatience, and that if he does not bear it, impatience will not return to him what is lost nor remove the hardship from him; that what is decreed has no way to be averted, and what is not decreed has no way to be attained; so impatience harms him more than it benefits him. Some wise people said:

"The intelligent person at the descent of calamity does what the fool does after a month," as it has been said:

"The matter leads to another, so its end becomes its beginning."

So if the end of the matter is patience, and the servant is not praised for impatience, how good it is for him to face the matter at its beginning with what the fool would turn his back on at its end. Some wise people said: whoever does not bear with the patience of the noble will forget like beasts forget. The noble looks at the calamity; if he sees that impatience will reverse it or repel it, then impatience may benefit him, but if impatience does not benefit him, he makes the calamity into two calamities.

As for the base person, he bears by compulsion, for he circles the courtyard of impatience and sees that it brings him no benefit, so he bears like one bound for a beating. Also, the noble bears in obedience to the Merciful, while the base bears in obedience to Satan. So the base are the most patient of people in obedience to their desires and lusts, and the least patient in obedience to their Lord. He bears with perfect patience in spending in obedience to Satan, yet cannot bear spending in obedience to Allah even for the smallest thing. He bears the hardships of enduring for the sake of his self's desire, in pleasing his enemy, yet cannot bear the least hardship in pleasing his Lord. He bears what is said about his honor in sin, yet cannot bear what is said about his honor when he is harmed for Allah; rather he flees from enjoining good and forbidding evil, fearing that he will be spoken of in his honor for the sake of Allah. He spends his honor in the desire of his self and its pleasure, enduring what is said about him, and likewise he bears humiliating himself and his standing for his self's desire and aim, but cannot bear humbling himself for Allah's pleasure and obedience. So he is the most patient of all in humiliation in obedience to Satan and the desires of the self, and the most incapable of all in bearing that for Allah.

This is the greatest baseness, and its possessor is not noble before Allah, nor will he stand with the people of nobility when they are called on the Day of Resurrection before all witnesses, that the assembly may know who is most worthy of nobility today: "Where are the God-fearing?"

Al-Nahhas said: this is an error according to the grammarians, because when one begins with the oath and the speech depends on it, there must be an answer.

(A subtle point)

Consider the surahs that begin with single letters: how you find the surah built upon the words of that letter. Among them is (Qaf), and the surah is built upon words containing the letter qaf: mention of the Qur'an, mention of creation, repetition of speech and its returning again and again, nearness to the son of Adam, the two angels receiving the servant's speech, mention of the Watcher, mention of the driver and the companion, being cast into Hell, the advance of threat, mention of the pious, mention of the heart, the generations, and the search through the lands, mention of "qawl" (speech) twice, the cleaving of the earth and the casting of firm mountains into it, the towering palm trees and provision, mention of a people, and the realization of the threat.

(Section: On the difference between the patience of the noble and the patience of the base)

Everyone must bear some of what they dislike, either by choice or by compulsion.

The noble person bears by choice, knowing the good outcome of patience, that he will be praised for it and blamed for impatience, and that if he does not bear it, impatience will not return to him what is lost nor remove the hardship from him; that what is decreed has no way to be averted, and what is not decreed has no way to be attained; so impatience harms him more than it benefits him. Some wise people said:

"The intelligent person at the descent of calamity does what the fool does after a month," as it has been said:

"The matter leads to another, so its end becomes its beginning."

So if the end of the matter is patience, and the servant is not praised for impatience, how good it is for him to face the matter at its beginning with what the fool would turn his back on at its end. Some wise people said: whoever does not bear with the patience of the noble will forget like beasts forget. The noble looks at the calamity; if he sees that impatience will reverse it or repel it, then impatience may benefit him, but if impatience does not benefit him, he makes the calamity into two calamities.

As for the base person, he bears by compulsion, for he circles the courtyard of impatience and sees that it brings him no benefit, so he bears like one bound for a beating. Also, the noble bears in obedience to the Merciful, while the base bears in obedience to Satan. So the base are the most patient of people in obedience to their desires and lusts, and the least patient in obedience to their Lord. He bears with perfect patience in spending in obedience to Satan, yet cannot bear spending in obedience to Allah even for the smallest thing. He bears the hardships of enduring for the sake of his self's desire, in pleasing his enemy, yet cannot bear the least hardship in pleasing his Lord. He bears what is said about his honor in sin, yet cannot bear what is said about his honor when he is harmed for Allah; rather he flees from enjoining good and forbidding evil, fearing that he will be spoken of in his honor for the sake of Allah. He spends his honor in the desire of his self and its pleasure, enduring what is said about him, and likewise he bears humiliating himself and his standing for his self's desire and aim, but cannot bear humbling himself for Allah's pleasure and obedience. So he is the most patient of all in humiliation in obedience to Satan and the desires of the self, and the most incapable of all in bearing that for Allah.

This is the greatest baseness, and its possessor is not noble before Allah, nor will he stand with the people of nobility when they are called on the Day of Resurrection before all witnesses, that the assembly may know who is most worthy of nobility today: "Where are the God-fearing?"

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 38, verse 24:

Concerning His Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him), He says: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned (in repentance)﴾.

Inabah (turning back in repentance, al-inabah) is returning to Allah and the heart's motives and pulls turning away from everything else toward Him. It includes both love and awe, for the one who turns in repentance (munib) loves the One he turns to, humbles himself before Him, is reverent, and abases himself. People differ in their inabah in degrees. Some turn to Allah by returning from transgressions and sins; this inabah springs from contemplating the threat (wa'id), and what drives it is knowledge, awe and caution. Others turn to Him by entering into various kinds of worship and acts of drawing near to Him; they strive in them with their utmost effort, and the performance of acts of obedience and various kinds of drawing near has been made beloved to them. This inabah springs from hope, contemplating the promise and the reward, and love for Allah's honour. These are more open of soul than the first category and more expansive of breast, and the side of hope and contemplation of mercy and favour predominates in them. Otherwise, each of the two groups turns in repentance by both matters together, but the fear of these people is subsumed within their hope, so they turn by means of acts of worship, while the hope of the first people is subsumed within their fear, so their inabah is by abandoning transgressions. Among them is one who turns to Allah through supplication, prayer, dependence on Him, desire, and asking Him for all needs.

The source of this inabah is witnessing (shuhud) Allah's grace, favour, richness, generosity and power. They place their needs upon Him and hang their hopes on Him. Their turning to Him from this aspect, together with their upholding of the commands and prohibitions, is their inabah; but their special inabah is from this aspect. As for deeds, they were not granted special inabah in them. Their hope in the one they turn to in times of hardship and distress is only an inabah of compulsion, not an inabah of choice, like the state of those about whom Allah said: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you invoke leave you except Him﴾ [al-Isra: 67].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Ankabut: 65].

All of these may have their spirits turned away from Allah, glorified is He, and averted from Him toward a natural, soulful familiarity that has come between them and their turning, in their essence, to their worshipped and true God. Their spirits are inclined toward other than Him, yet they have a turning toward Him according to their faith in Him and their knowledge of Him.

The highest kind of inabah is the turning of the whole spirit to Him, due to the intensity of pure love, which makes them independent of everything other than their Beloved and their Worshipped. When their spirits turned to Him, nothing among them differed from the inabah, for all the limbs are its subjects and its dominion, following the spirit. When the spirit turned in its essence to Him, with the turning of a sincere lover whose love leaves no vein or joint without a settled love for the beloved, all the powers and bodily members turned as well: the heart turned in love, submission, humility and abasement.

The intellect turned by being moved by the commands and prohibitions of the Beloved, by submitting to them, and by ruling by them alone, so that no doubt or objection remained in it to stand between it and them. The soul turned by compliance, by stripping off its soulful habits, blameworthy character and corrupt desires; it submitted to the command, humbly, calling to it, preferring it over everything else. No desire remained in it to oppose the command, and it went out of its own management and choice, entrusting itself to its Master, content with His decree and submitting to His judgement.

It has been said: the servant's management of himself is the last of the blameworthy qualities of the soul.

The body turned by deeds, by performing its obligations and recommended acts in the most perfect manner. Every limb and member turned in its own particular inabah, so that in this servant who turns there remains no vein or joint without an inabah and a return to the true Beloved, for every love other than His is a torment to its possessor, even if it is sweet at its beginnings, for it is torment in its consequences. Thus the inabah of the servant, even for an hour of his life, in this pure form, is more beneficial to him and greater in fruit than the inabah of many years by others. So where is this one's inabah compared with the inabah of those before him?

That is the grace of Allah which He gives to whom He wills. Rather, this spirit is always turning, and even if the witnessing of its inabah is hidden from him by preoccupation, it lies within it like the fire's latency in the flint.

As for those of the earlier inabahs: if one of them turns for an hour through supplication, remembrance and entreaty, his soul, spirit, heart and intellect still have glances away from the One to whom he turned; he turns with a part of himself for an hour, then leaves that and turns again to the motives of his own self and nature.

And Allah is the Granter of success and the Helper; there is no lord other than Him and no god besides Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 25:

Allah, the Exalted, said concerning His Prophet Dawud (David): ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾

So "zulfa" (nearness) is the station of closeness, and "husn al-ma'ab" (a good return) is the goodness of reward and recompense.

(Section)

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated to me: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr narrated to me: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Malik ibn Dinar, concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾

He said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, a lofty pulpit will be commanded and placed in Paradise. Then it will be called out: "O Dawud, glorify Me with that beautiful, melodious voice with which you used to glorify Me in the abode of the world." He said: So the voice of Dawud will outdo the delight of the people of the Gardens. This is the meaning of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾

ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad said in Kitab al-Zuhd (The Book of Asceticism) of his father: ʿAli ibn Muslim al-Tusi narrated to me: Sayyar narrated to me: Ja'far narrated to us: Malik ibn Dinar narrated to us, concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾

He said: Allah, glory be to Him, will station Dawud near the Throne's leg, and say:

"O Dawud, glorify Me today with that beautiful, melodious voice." He will say: "My Lord, how can I glorify You when You have taken it from me in the abode of the world?"

He said: Then the Mighty and Majestic will say: "Indeed I return it to you." He said: So it will be returned to him, and his voice will increase.

He said: So the voice of Dawud will outdo the delight of the people of Paradise.

**The Danger of Assuming the Judgeship**

For this reason, the warning and admonition concerning the judge (qadi) is more severe than anything comparable concerning the mufti (one who issues legal opinions). Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related it from the hadith of Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her): that the judges were mentioned in her presence, and she said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say:

"The just judge will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and he will suffer such severity of reckoning that he will wish he had never judged between two people, even over a single date."

Al-Sha'bi related from Masruq, from Abdullah, who traced it back (to the Prophet ﷺ):

"There is no ruler who judges between people except that an angel is assigned to him, seizing him by the nape of his neck until he stands him at the edge of Hell. Then he raises his head to Allah. If He commands that he be cast down, the angel casts him into a pit of forty autumns (years)."

In the Sunan (collections) is the hadith of Ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Judges are of three kinds: two are in the Fire and one is in Paradise. A man who knew the truth and judged by it is in Paradise. A man who judged between people in ignorance is in the Fire. And a man who knew the truth but acted unjustly is in the Fire."

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Woe to the judge of those on earth from the Judge of those in heaven, on the day they meet Him, except for one who commanded justice, judged by the truth, did not judge according to whim, nor according to kinship, nor out of desire or fear, and made the Book of Allah a mirror before his eyes."

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said:

"Whoever seeks the judgeship of the Muslims until he obtains it, and then his justice prevails over his injustice, will have Paradise. And whoever has his injustice prevail over his justice, will have the Fire."

In the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, from Ata, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Allah is with the judge so long as he does not act unjustly. When he acts unjustly, Allah disassociates Himself from him, and Satan clings to him."

In the same work, from the hadith of Husayn al-Mu'allim, from al-Shaybani, from Ibn Abi Awfa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed Allah is with the judge so long as he does not act unjustly. When he acts unjustly, He leaves him to himself."

In the Four Sunan, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever appoints a judge among the Muslims has slaughtered himself without a knife." In the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Woe to the rulers, woe to the stewards, woe to the trustees! On the Day of Resurrection, people will wish that their forelocks had been hung from the Pleiades, swaying between heaven and earth, and that they had never held any office."

The falsehood they assumed is not the combining of two contradictories. Rather, what they assumed is that there is no law, no recompense, no command and no prohibition, no reward and no punishment. So He informed that creating it for other than that is the falsehood from which He is exalted. That is the truth for which it was created, and it is Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), and its right, its recompense, and the recompense of whoever denies it and associates others with his Lord.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 28:

This is a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkar), which indicates that this is ugly in itself, a reprehensible thing that the intellects and natural dispositions (fitar) reject. "Do you think that it befits us, or that it is good for us to do it?" So He, glorified is He, denounced it as a denunciation that alerts the intellect and the natural disposition to its ugliness, and that it is not fitting for God to be ascribed to it.

[Section: The wisdom in distinguishing between one time and another time, and one place and another place, in excellence]

As for his saying: "He singled out some times and places and preferred some of them over others, although they are equal, etc."

Then the first premise is true, and the second is false.

He preferred some of them over others only because of distinctive qualities that subsisted in them, which necessitated the specification. God, glorified is He, does not single out anything except by a specifying cause, but that cause may be manifest and may be hidden. The sharing of times and places in the name of time and place is like the sharing of animal in the name of animality and human in the name of humanity, and indeed of all genera in the meaning that encompasses them.

That does not necessitate their equality in themselves. Things that differ share many matters, and things that agree differ in many matters. God, glorified is He, is too wise and too knowing to prefer one like over another like in every respect without a quality that necessitates preferring it. This is impossible in His creation and command, just as He, glorified is He, does not distinguish between two alike in every respect; His wisdom and justice reject both.

He, glorified is He, has declared Himself free of whoever supposes this of Him, and denounced his false claim and made it a reprehensible judgment. If what these people say were permissible of Him, His proofs and arguments would be nullified, for they are founded on the principle that the judgment on a thing is the judgment on its like, and on not equating between two different things. So He does not make the righteous like the wicked, nor the believers like the disbelievers, nor one who obeys Him like one who disobeys Him, nor the knower like the ignorant. Upon this is founded the recompense: it is His cosmic and religious judgment, and His recompense, which is His reward and punishment. By this lesson is drawn, for its sake parables are struck, and the reports of the prophets and their nations are related to us.

It suffices to refute this abandoned doctrine, which is among the most corrupt doctrines of the world, that it entails the equality of the essence of Gabriel with the essence of Iblis, and the essences of the prophets with the essences of their enemies, and the place of the Ancient House (the Ka'bah) with the place of latrines and the houses of devils, and that there is no difference between these essences in reality.

These essences were distinguished from one another only by what they were distinguished by, through the sheer will that preponderates one like over another like without a cause. Rather, they said this about all bodies, that they are alike: the body of musk, according to them, is equal to the body of urine and excrement, and it is distinguished from it only by an accidental quality. The body of ice, according to them, is equal in reality to the body of fire. This is among the things they went out with from clear reason, and they defied sense perception in it, and the majority of intelligent people from the adherents of the religions and sects opposed them in it. God did not equate the body of the heaven with the body of the earth, nor the body of fire with the body of water, nor the body of air with the body of stone. The disputants on this have nothing but sharing in a general matter, namely accepting division, the existence of the three dimensions, sensory indication, and similar things, which do not necessitate similarity, let alone sameness. And success is from God.

[Section: The Benefits of Pondering the Qur'an and Contemplating Its Meanings]

As for contemplation (ta'ammul) of the Qur'an, it is directing the gaze of the heart toward its meanings and gathering the mind to ponder (tadabbur) and understand it. This is the purpose for which it was sent down, not merely reciting it without understanding or pondering. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A Book which We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾ [Sad: 29]

Allah the Exalted also says: ﴿Then do they not ponder the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then have they not pondered the word?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 68]

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "The Qur'an was sent down to be pondered and acted upon, so take its recitation as a deed."

There is nothing more beneficial to the servant in his life in this world and in the Hereafter, and nearer to his salvation, than pondering the Qur'an, prolonging contemplation of it, and gathering the mind upon the meanings of its verses. For it makes the servant acquainted with the landmarks of good and evil in their entirety, and with their paths, causes, ends, fruits, and the final outcome of their people. It places in his hand the keys to the treasures of happiness and beneficial knowledge, establishes the foundations of faith in his heart, raises its structure, strengthens its pillars, and shows him in his heart the image of this world and the Hereafter, Paradise and Hell. It brings him into the presence of past nations, shows him the days of Allah concerning them, makes him perceive the places of lessons, and makes him witness the justice and grace of Allah. It makes him know His Essence, His names, His attributes and His acts, what He loves and what He hates, His straight path that leads to Him, what awaits those who travel it after arrival and coming before Him, the obstacles of the road and its dangers, and it makes him know the self and its attributes, the things that corrupt deeds and the things that correct them. It makes him know the way of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, their deeds, their states and their marks, the ranks of the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness, the divisions of creation, their gathering in what they gather upon, and their separation in what they separate over.

In sum, it makes him know the Lord to whom he is called, the path of reaching Him, and the honour that awaits him when he comes before Him.

And in contrast to that, it makes him know three other things: what Satan calls to, the paths that lead to it, and the humiliation and punishment that await whoever responds to his call after arriving at it.

These are six matters which it is essential for the servant to know, to witness and to contemplate. It makes him witness the Hereafter as though he were in it, and makes him absent from this world as though he were not in it. It distinguishes for him between truth and falsehood in everything over which the world has disagreed. It shows him truth as truth and falsehood as falsehood, and gives him a criterion (furqan) and a light by which he distinguishes between guidance and misguidance, error and right direction. It gives him strength in his heart, life, expansiveness, openness, joy and happiness, so that he becomes in one state while people are in another.

The meanings of the Qur'an revolve around tawhid (the oneness of God) and its proofs, knowledge of Allah and what belongs to Him of the attributes of perfection, and what is exalted above the marks of deficiency; around faith in the Messengers, the mention of the proofs of their truthfulness and the evidences of the soundness of their prophethood, and the explanation of their rights and the rights of the One who sent them; around faith in His angels, who are His messengers in His creation and command, who manage affairs by His permission and will, and what they have been entrusted with regarding the affairs of the higher and lower worlds, and what is specific to the human species among them, from the moment he settles in his mother's womb until the day he meets his Lord and comes before Him; and around faith in the Last Day and what Allah has prepared in it for His friends of the abode of absolute bliss, in which they feel no pain, distress or disturbance, and what He has prepared for His enemies of the abode of severe punishment, which is mixed with no joy, ease, comfort or delight.

These are described in the most complete and clearest detail. They also cover the details of command and prohibition, of the divine law and decree, of the lawful and the unlawful, of admonitions and lessons, of stories and parables, of causes and wisdoms, and of beginnings and ends in His creation and His command.

So its meanings never cease to rouse the servant toward his Lord with the beautiful promise, to warn him and make him fear with its threat of severe punishment, to urge him to be lean and light for the meeting of the heavy Day, to guide him through the darkness of opinions and sects to the right path, to restrain him from plunging into the roads of innovations and falsehoods, to incite him to increase in blessings by thanking his noble Lord, to show him the limits of the lawful and the unlawful and to stop him at them lest he transgress them and fall into long hardship, to fix his heart against deviation and turning away from the truth and changing, to make easy for him the difficult affairs and steep obstacles with the utmost ease, and to call out to him whenever his resolve weakens and he slackens in his journey: "The caravan has advanced and the guide has passed you by! Hasten, hasten, depart, depart!" It drives him forward and walks before him as the guide walks. And whenever an ambush from the ambushes of the enemy comes out upon him, or a highwayman from the highwaymen, it calls out to him: "Beware, beware!" So seek refuge in Allah, ask Him for help, and say: "Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

In contemplating the Qur'an, pondering it and understanding it, there are multiples upon multiples of the wisdoms and benefits we have mentioned.

In sum, it is the greatest of treasures, and its talisman (tilsam) is to dive deep with thought to the bottom of its meanings.

Purify your heart from anything other than its gardens, for its meadows are lawful to every one who seeks to be pure;
And understanding is the talisman of its treasure of knowledge, so aim at the talisman and you will attain its treasure.
Do not fear the innovations of the people nor the events they bring, as long as you are within the protection and guard of the Book.
Whoever has the Book as his guardian and shield will not fear the thrust of the enemy nor its stab.
Do not fear their doubts, but when they confront you, advance with its victory and its might.
By Allah, no man has feared their doubts except from the weakness of heart and inability in him.
Alas for a lame he-goat that seeks to challenge the lion's cub with its running and its leaping!
And a smoke of dung that rises toward the sun, seeking to blind its eye as it spreads into its brightness.
And a coward of a weaponless heart who has tried to frighten a horseman armed and brandishing his spear.

**Chapter: Jealousy (ghayra) is the collapse of forbearance out of protectiveness, and the constriction of patience out of prized possession.**

The author of *al-Manazil* said: Chapter on Jealousy (ghayra). God the Exalted said, relating about His Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him): ﴿Bring them back to me.” Then he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks﴾ [Sad 38:33].

The way he cites this verse as evidence is that Sulayman (peace be upon him) loved horses.

When they were displayed before him, his admiration of them and his gazing at them distracted him from the afternoon prayer, until the sun had set behind the veil.

Then jealousy for God (ghayra lillah) overcame him concerning the horses, since his admiration of them and his gazing at them had absorbed him away from serving his Master and fulfilling His right.

So he said: “Bring them back to me,” and he began to strike their necks and hocks with the sword out of jealousy for God.

He said: Jealousy is the collapse of forbearance out of protectiveness, and the constriction of patience out of prized possession.

That is, the jealous person is unable to tolerate what distracts him from his beloved and what screens him from Him. He is protective of the beloved, meaning he is stingy with him, lest he replace him with something else. This stinginess is, for true lovers, pure generosity.

As for the constriction of patience out of prized possession, it means that his capacity for patience becomes constricted regarding his beloved. This is the patience that is not blamed, among all kinds of patience, or else it is what is part of its means. What drives him to this constriction is his exaggerated valuing of his beloved, and this is prized possession (nafasa). Because of his rivalry (munafasa) and his desire, he does not permit himself to be patient concerning him.

Rivalry (munafasa) is the completeness of desire for a thing and the prevention of others from it, if participation in it is not praised. It is a competing to attain it, if sharing in it is praised. God the Exalted said: ﴿And for this let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 83:26].

Between rivalry and ghibta (envious admiration) there is both a commonality and a difference, and between them and envy (hasad) there is also a commonality and a difference.

Rivalry involves competition, striving, and eagerness. Envy indicates the baseness and incapacity of the envier. Otherwise, compete with the one you envy, for that is more beneficial to you than his envy, as it has been said:

*When the qualities of a man please you,*
*then become like him, and what pleases you will be yours.*

*Those noble and generous things, when you come to them,*
*there is no chamberlain there to bar you.*

Ghibta includes a kind of wonder and joy for the one who is envied, and an admiration of his condition.

(Section)

The jurists have differed concerning the fay' (spoils gained without battle). Was it the property of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), to dispose of as he wished, or was it not his property?

This is one of two opinions within the school of Ahmad (ibn Hanbal) and others.

What his Sunnah and his guidance indicate is that he disposed of it by command: he placed it where God commanded him, and distributed it among those whom he was commanded to distribute it to. He did not dispose of it as an owner does by his desire and will, giving to whom he loved and withholding from whom he loved. Rather, he disposed of it as a commanded servant does, carrying out what his master and lord had ordered him, giving to whom he was ordered to give and withholding from whom he was ordered to withhold.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) made this explicit when he said:

"By God, I do not give anything to anyone, nor do I withhold it from anyone. I am only a distributor; I place it where I am commanded."

So his giving, his withholding and his distribution were by mere command. God, glory be to Him, gave him the choice between being a servant-messenger and being a king-messenger, and he chose to be a servant-messenger.

The difference between them is that the servant-messenger does not act except by the command of his master and sender, whereas the king-messenger has the right to give to whom he wills and to withhold from whom he wills, as God, the Exalted, said to the king-messenger Solomon: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account﴾ [Sad: 39].

That is: give to whom you wish, and withhold from whom you wish; We will not call you to account. This station is the one that was offered to our Prophet (ﷺ), but he turned away from it to what is higher than it, namely the station of pure servanthood, in which its possessor's conduct is confined to the command of the master in every small and great matter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 44:

He praised His servant Job with the finest praise for his patience, saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient. How excellent a servant he was! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Us).﴾

By calling him "an excellent servant" on account of having found him patient, He indicates that whoever does not show patience when tried is indeed a wretched servant.

(Benefit)

Complaining to Allah, the Exalted, does not contradict patience in any way. Allah, the Exalted, said of Job: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient. How excellent a servant he was! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Us).﴾

Yet He also reported his complaint to Him in his words: ﴿Harm has touched me﴾, and He reported of His Prophet Jacob that he vowed to himself beautiful patience. A prophet, when he says something, fulfils it, together with his saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾, and He did not make that a deficiency in his patience.

It is not to be overlooked that other than this is among the empty notions of certain people, as one of them said when Job said: ﴿Harm has touched me﴾:

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾, and He did not say "patient in tribulation" (ṣabūran) when he said ﴿harm has touched me﴾.

Another of them said: Job did not say "have mercy on me," but said ﴿You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾, so he added nothing beyond reporting his own state and describing his Lord.

Another of them said: He only complained of the touch of harm when his tongue became too weak to remember (God), so he complained of the harm of weakness in remembrance, not the harm of sickness and pain.

Another of them said: This statement was drawn out of him so that he might serve as an example for the weak of this community.

It seems that this speaker held that complaining to Allah contradicts patience, and he erred in the most hideous of errors. What contradicts patience is his complaining, not complaining to Him. Allah tests His servant in order to hear his supplication and his entreaty, and his complaint to Him, and He does not love stoic endurance before Him. What is most beloved to Him is the breaking of His servant's heart before Him, his humbling himself to Him, and his displaying his weakness, his neediness, his incapacity and his little patience. So beware with utmost caution of displaying stoic endurance before Him; rather, hold to humble supplication, meekness, and showing incapacity, neediness, lowliness and weakness, for His mercy is closer to this heart than the hand is to the mouth.

(Section: On some people's use of this verse to argue for the permissibility of legal stratagems [ḥiyal])

They said: Allah, the Exalted, said to His Prophet Job, peace be upon him, when he had sworn that he would flog his wife one hundred times: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigth) and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾.

Saʿīd reported from Qatādah: His wife had offered him something in a matter, and Iblīs wanted something from her, so he said to her: "If only you spoke such and such a word?"

Hunger had driven her to it. The Prophet of Allah swore that if Allah healed him he would flog her one hundred lashes.

He said: So he was commanded to take a palm-stalk containing ninety-nine shoots, the palm-stalk being to complete the hundred, and strike her once with it.

So Allah fulfilled His Prophet's oath and lightened the burden on his community.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr said: Iblīs met her and said to her: "By Allah, if your husband spoke one word, every harm would be lifted from him, and his wealth and children would return to him." She informed Job, and he said: "Woe to you! That is the enemy of Allah. Your likeness is only that of the adulterous woman: when her lover brings her something, she accepts it and admits him; and if he brings her nothing, she drives him away and shuts her door against him.

When Allah gave us wealth and children, we believed in Him, and when He takes back what is His from us, we disbelieve in Him.

If Allah restores me from my illness, I will surely flog you one hundred times." So Allah gave him a ruling of what he had reported: that he should take a ḍigth, which is a bundle of things, such as moist palm-spathes and sticks and the like, which stand upon a stalk, and strike her with it once.

This is a teaching from Him, the Exalted, to His servants on escaping sins and the way out of hardship with the easiest of means, and this is our basis in the matter of ḥiyal, for we analogised on this and made it a principle.

(Section)

Those who reject ḥiyal said:

Ḥiyal are of three kinds:

A kind which is an act of nearness and obedience, and it is among the best of deeds in the sight of Allah, the Exalted.

A kind which is permissible and lawful, with no blame upon the one who does it or upon the one who leaves it, and whether doing it is preferable to leaving it, or the reverse, follows its benefit.

A kind which is forbidden and a deception of Allah and His Messenger, entailing the abolition of what He made obligatory, the nullification of what He legislated, and the making lawful of what He forbade.

The denunciation by the Salaf, the Imams, and the people of ḥadīth is directed only at this kind.

For the stratagem (ḥīlah) is not blamed absolutely, nor praised absolutely, and its wording does not imply praise or blame, although in custom its use has become predominant for the subtle paths to attaining an aim, such that it is not perceived except through some kind of cleverness and astuteness.

More specific than this is restricting it to what is blameworthy of that, and this is the prevalent usage of the jurists who reject ḥiyal, for people of custom have a freedom in restricting general terms to some of their referents and confining their absolute senses to some of their types.

The word ḥīlah is a form (fiʿlah) from ḥawl, which is change from one state to another. It is of the waw-root, its original form being ḥawlah; the waw was made quiescent and the preceding letter was given a kasra, so it was changed into a yā', as in mīzān, mīqāt, and mīʿād.

In al-Muḥkam it is said: al-ḥawl, al-ḥayl, al-ḥiwal, al-ḥawlah, al-ḥīlah, al-ḥuwayl, al-maḥālah, al-maḥāl, al-iḥtiyāl, al-taḥawwul, and al-taḥayyul: all of these mean shrewdness, quality of insight, and capability in the manner of handling. It says: al-ḥawl, al-ḥayl, and al-ḥiyalāt are plurals of ḥīlah; a man is ḥawal, ḥawalah, ḥawl, ḥawwalah, ḥawālā, ḥawlūl, and ḥawwalā: one who is intensely skilled at ḥiyal. And how skilled he is, and how skilled he is, and he is more skilled than you, and ḥayyal. End quote.

So ḥīlah is a form from ḥawl, meaning change from state to state, and whoever seeks to accomplish a matter he wishes to do or to escape from, what he devises to that end is a ḥīlah by which he reaches it.

Thus ḥīlah is judged by the matter it is devised against, whether permitting or forbidding, benefit or harm, obedience or disobedience.

If the aim is a good matter, the ḥīlah is good. If the aim is ugly, the ḥīlah is ugly.

If the aim is obedience and nearness, the ḥīlah concerning it is likewise.

If the aim is disobedience and transgression, the ḥīlah concerning it is likewise.

When the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, lest you make lawful the prohibitions of Allah, the Exalted, by the slightest of stratagems."

It became in the usage of the jurists, when used without qualification, a reference to those stratagems by which prohibitions are made lawful, like the stratagems of the Jews.

Every stratagem that entails the forfeiture of a right of Allah or of a human being is among those by which prohibitions are made lawful.

A parallel to this is the word khidāʿ (deception), which is divided into praiseworthy and blameworthy: if it is in truth, it is praiseworthy, and if it is in falsehood, it is blameworthy.

From the praiseworthy kind is His, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, saying: "War is deception."

And His saying in the ḥadīth narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others:

"All lying is recorded against the son of Adam, except three kinds: a man who lied to his wife to please her, a man who lied between two people to reconcile them, and a man who lied in the deception of war."

From the blameworthy kind is His saying in the ḥadīth of ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ:

"The people of the Fire are five," and he mentioned among them "a man who does not rise in the morning or the evening except that he is deceiving you concerning your family and your property."

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive only themselves, and they perceive (it) not﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9].

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if they intend to deceive you, then sufficient for you is Allah﴾ [al-Anfāl: 62].

(Section)

Having known that, there is no difficulty that a person may display a statement or act whose purpose is a righteous aim, even if its apparent meaning differs from what is intended, if there is a religious benefit in it, such as repelling injustice from himself or from another, or nullifying a forbidden stratagem.

What is forbidden is only that one intends by the lawful contracts other than what Allah and His Messenger legislated them for.

Then he becomes one who deceives Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, a plotter against His religion, a schemer against His law, for his aim is the attainment, through that stratagem, of the thing which Allah and His Messenger forbade, and the forfeiture, through that stratagem, of what He made obligatory.

(Section)

As for the saying of Allah, the Exalted, to Job, peace be upon him: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ [Ṣād: 44].

It is strange that one who argues from this verse also holds that if a man swears that he will strike someone ten lashes, then gathers them and strikes him with them in a single blow, he has not fulfilled his oath.

This is the view of the companions of Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, and the companions of Aḥmad.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: If he knows that all of them touched him, he has fulfilled his oath; if he knows that they did not touch him, he has not fulfilled it; and if he is in doubt, he is not in breach. And if this were what fulfils the swearer's oath, it would have dropped from the adulterer, the slanderer, and the drinker the multiplicity of strokes, by gathering a hundred lashes or eighty for him and striking him with them in a single blow.

This is only valid in the case of the sick person, as Imam Aḥmad said concerning a sick man upon whom the hadd was due: "He is struck with a bunch (ʿithkāl) whereby the hadd is dropped from him."

He argued by what he related from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah, who said: "There was among our tents a weak, deceptive man, and the clan was not aware until he was upon one of their maidservants, committing indecency with her. Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, and that man was a Muslim. He said: 'Strike him his hadd.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he is weaker than you think; if we struck him a hundred times, we would kill him.' He said: 'Take for him a ʿithkāl containing a hundred shoots, then strike him with it once.' And they did so."

As for the story of Job, it has subtle jurisprudence. His wife, out of her great eagerness for his well-being and his deliverance from his affliction, was seeking for him a remedy with what she could. When Satan met her and said what he said, she informed Job, peace be upon him, of that. He said: "It is Satan." Then he swore: "If Allah heals me, I will surely strike her one hundred lashes." She was thus excused and well-intentioned in his matter, and there was no expiation in their law, for if there had been an expiation in their law, he would have turned to expiation and would not have needed to strike her. So the oath was binding upon them, like the hadds. It has been established that the one subject to a hadd, if he is excused, is lightened for, by gathering for him a hundred shoots or a hundred lashes and striking him with them in a single blow. Job's wife was excused; she did not know that the one who addressed her was Satan, and she only intended kindness, so she did not deserve punishment. Allah therefore gave His Prophet Job, peace be upon him, a ruling that he should deal with her as with one who is excused. This was alongside her gentleness with him and her kindness to him. Thus Allah combined for him fulfilment of his oath and kindness to his wife, who was well-intentioned, excused, and did not deserve punishment. The agreement of the Qur'anic text in the story of Job, peace be upon him, with the Sunnah's text regarding the weak man who committed fornication is thus evident, so it should not be stretched beyond its proper place.

If it is said: then say the same of the parallel case, of one who swears that he will strike his wife or his slave-girl a hundred times, and they are both excused and free of fault: that he fulfils it by gathering that into one blow with a hundred shoots.

It is answered: Allah has made for him a way out through expiation, and it is obligatory upon him to expiate for his oath. He must not disobey Allah by fulfilling his oath here, and it is not lawful for him to fulfil it in this case; rather, his fulfilling it here is breaking it together with the expiation. And it is not lawful for him to strike her, neither separately nor together.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verses 45–47 (part 1 of 3):

Al-aydi (the hands) means strength and resolve in the cause of God, and al-absar (the eyes) means insight into the command of God.
The expressions of the early generations (al-salaf) revolve around this.
Ibn Abbas said: "Possessors of strength in obedience to God and knowledge of God."
Al-Kalbi said: "Possessors of strength in worship, and insight into it."
Mujahid said: "Al-aydi: strength in obedience to God. Al-absar: sight into the truth."
Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Al-aydi: strength in action. Al-absar: their insight into what they are in of their religion."
It has come in a hadith mursal (a hadith whose chain drops the Companion) that: "God loves the piercing insight when doubts arrive, and He loves the complete intellect when desires descend."
So by the completeness of intellect and patience, the trial of desire is repelled, and by the completeness of insight and certainty, the trial of doubt is repelled. And God is the One sought for help.

God's saying: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Home﴾.
That is: We singled them out with a distinction, which is the good mention by which they are remembered in this abode. This is the "tongue of truthfulness" that Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be peace, asked for when he said: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 84].
He, glorified and exalted, also said about him and his descendants: ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy and made for them a tongue of truth, high and exalted﴾ [Maryam 50].
And He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And We raised high your mention﴾ [al-Sharh 4].
So the followers of the messengers have a share of that according to their inheritance of their obedience and their following of them, and whoever opposed them is far from that according to their opposition and disobedience.

He said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn, "The Path of the Two Emigrations"):
In this verse, He, glorified be He, informs of what His prophets and messengers were purified for, namely their being singled out for the Hereafter. There are two views concerning it:
The first is that the meaning is: We removed from their hearts the love of this world, its remembrance, preferring it, and working for it.
The second view: We purified them with the best of what is in the Hereafter, and We singled them out with it above all the worlds.

[Section: Sins Blind the Heart]
Among its punishments is that it blinds the heart. If it does not blind it, it weakens its insight, without fail. This has already been explained: that it weakens it, without fail. When the heart becomes blind and weak, it misses the knowledge of guidance and the strength to implement it in itself and in others, in proportion to the weakness and strength of its insight.
The human perfection rests on two principles: knowing the truth from falsehood, and preferring it over falsehood.
The ranks of creatures before God, in this world and the Hereafter, differ only in proportion to their differing ranks in these two matters. These are the two qualities by which God, glorified be He, praised His prophets, in His saying: ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, possessors of strength and insight﴾ [Sad 45].
So "al-aydi" means strength in implementing the truth, and "al-absar" means insight in the religion. He described them with the completeness of perceiving the truth and the completeness of implementing it. People are divided in this station into four categories, and these are the noblest categories of creation and the most honored by God, the Exalted.
The second category is the opposite of these: one who has no insight into the religion and no strength to implement the truth. They are the majority of this creation. They are those whose sight is a speck in the eyes, a fever for the spirits, and a sickness of the hearts. They constrict the abodes, make prices high, and no benefit is gained from their company except shame and disgrace.
The third category is one who has insight into the truth and knowledge of it, but is weak, having no strength to implement it or to call to it. This is the condition of the weak believer, and the strong believer is better and more beloved to God than him.
The fourth category is one who has strength, determination, and resolve, but is weak in insight into the religion. He can hardly distinguish between the friends of the Merciful and the friends of Satan. Rather, he considers every black (date) a date and every white a fat, he takes the swelling for fat, and the beneficial medicine for poison.
None of these is fit for the leadership in religion, nor is he a place for it, except the first category. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah 24].
So He, glorified be He, informed that by patience and certainty they attained leadership in religion. These are the ones whom God, glorified be He, excepted from the lost. He swore by al-Asr, which is the time in which the lost and the winners strive, that whoever other than them is among the lost. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who believed and did righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [al-Asr 1–3].
They did not suffice with knowing the truth and being patient upon it, until each of them advises the others to it, guides them to it, and urges them upon it.
If whoever is other than these is lost, it is known that sins and wrongdoings blind the insight of the heart, so it does not perceive the truth as it should. Its strength and resolve weaken, so it is not patient upon it. Indeed, it may keep recurring upon the heart until its perception is reversed just as its journey is reversed, so it perceives falsehood as truth and truth as falsehood, the good as evil and the evil as good. Thus it turns back in its journey and returns from its journey to God and the Last Abode, to a journey toward the dwelling of the falsifying souls, which are content with the worldly life, reassured by it, heedless of God and His signs, and have abandoned preparation for meeting Him. Even if the punishment for sins were only this alone, it would be enough to call one to abandon them and keep away from them. And God is the One sought for help.

This is like obedience, which illuminates the heart, polishes it, clears it, strengthens it, and firms it, until it becomes like a polished mirror in its brightness and clarity, filled with light. When Satan approaches it, he receives from its light what the eavesdropper receives from the piercing shooting stars. Satan flees from this heart more than the wolf flees from the lion. Indeed, its owner may throw down Satan so that he falls prostrate, and the devils gather around him, and one of them says to another: "What is his affair?"
It is said: "A human has struck him, and there is an evil eye from a human."
Poetry:
O glance from a heart of a free man, illuminated,
by which Satan nearly burns with the light.

Is this heart equal to a heart whose surroundings are dark, whose desires are divided, which Satan has taken as his homeland and prepared as his dwelling? When he wakes in the morning with its face, he greets it and says: "I ransom one who does not succeed in his world nor in his Hereafter."
Poetry:
Your companion in this world and in the gathering after it,
so you are a companion of mine in every place.
If you are in the abode of wretchedness, then I
and you are all in misery and humiliation.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion. And indeed, they avert them from the way, while they think they are guided. Until, when he comes to Us, he says: "Oh, I wish there were between me and you the distance of the two easts! How wretched is the companion." And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you will be sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf 36–39].

[Section: The Station of Purity]
The author of al-Manazil (the Stations) said:
The chapter of purity (al-safa'). God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen, the good﴾.
Purity (al-safa') is a name for freedom from turbidity. In this chapter, it is the falling away of fluctuation (al-talwin).
As for citing the verse, its aspect is that al-mustafa (the chosen) is derived from al-safwah.
It is the essence of a thing and its clarification from what mixes with it. From it: he chose the thing for himself, that is, he purified it from the mixture of another's share in it. From it also: al-safiyy, which is the portion that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to select for himself from the spoils. From it also: the pure thing, which is what is free from the turbidity of something else.
His saying: "Purity is a name for freedom from turbidity."
Freedom (al-bara'ah) is deliverance. And turbidity (al-kadar) is the mixing of the good with the bad.
His saying: "And in this chapter it is: the falling away of fluctuation."
Fluctuation (al-talwin) is hesitation and wavering, as it has been said:
Every day you change color;
leaving this is more beautiful for you.

[Degrees of Purity]
[The First Degree: Purity of Knowledge that Refines for Traveling the Path]
He said: "It has three degrees."
The first degree: purity of knowledge that refines for traveling the path, makes clear the utmost of striving, and corrects the resolve of the seeker.
The shaykh (the author of al-Manazil) mentioned three benefits for this degree.
The first benefit: knowledge that refines for traveling the path. This pure knowledge, which he pointed to, is the knowledge that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought.
Al-Junayd used to say constantly: "Our knowledge is bound by the Book and the Sunnah. Whoever does not memorize the Qur'an, write down the hadith, and gain understanding, is not to be followed."
Another of the knowers (al-'arifin) said: "Every truth that is not followed by the sharia (the revealed law) is disbelief."
Al-Junayd also said: "Our knowledge is intertwined with the hadith of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."
Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: "A witticism of the people passes through my heart, and I do not accept it except with two witnesses of justice, from the Book and the Sunnah."
Al-Nasrabadhi said: "The root of this path is adherence to the Book and the Sunnah, abandoning desires and innovations, following the early generations, and abandoning what later people have invented, and remaining upon what the first ones followed."
Some of this has already been mentioned.
So this pure knowledge, received from the niche of revelation and prophethood, refines its bearer for traveling the path of servitude. Its reality is: adopting the manners of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), inwardly and outwardly, and making him judge inwardly and outwardly, and standing where he stands with you and proceeding where he proceeds with you. Make him in place of your shaykh, to whom you have surrendered all your affair, secret and open, and whom you follow in all your conditions, standing with what he commands you, never opposing him. Thus you make the Messenger of God (ﷺ) your shaykh, imam, model, and judge, and you attach your heart to his noble heart and your spirituality to his spirituality, as the disciple attaches his spirituality to the spirituality of his shaykh. You respond to him when he calls you, stand when he stops you, proceed when he moves you, halt when he says so, descend when he descends, become angry at his anger, and be pleased with his pleasure. When he informs you about something, you consider it as if you saw it with your eye. When he informs you about God with a report, you consider it as if you heard it from God with your ear.
In sum: you make the Messenger your shaykh, teacher, educator, trainer, and instructor. You drop all intermediaries between you and him except in conveying, just as intermediaries drop between you and the Sender in servitude. No intermediary is established except in the arrival of His command, prohibition, and message to you.
These two stripping-away are the reality of the testimony that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger. God alone is the one worshipped and served, who deserves worship to the exclusion of all else. His messenger is the one obeyed and followed, the one guided by, who deserves obedience to the exclusion of all else. Whoever else is obeyed is only obeyed when the Messenger commands obedience to him, so he is obeyed as a follower of the source.
In sum: the path is blocked except for one who follows the traces of the Messenger (ﷺ) and imitates him outwardly and inwardly.
The traveler on other than this path does not toil in vain, for his share of his journey is only exhaustion, and his deeds are ﴿like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds God with him, and He pays him in full his account. And God is swift in account﴾ [al-Nur 39].
The traveler on this path does not toil in vain, for he arrives even if he crawls crawling. The followers of the Messenger (ﷺ): when their deeds sit them down, their resolves, their aspirations, and their following of their Prophet stand them up. As it has been said:
Who for me is like your gentle pace?
You walk slowly and arrive first.
And those who deviate from his path: when their deeds and efforts stand them up, their deviation from his path sits them down.
They in the night journey have not left their place,
and they have not moved from it, though they have grown weary.

His saying "and makes clear the utmost of striving": striving (al-jidd) is diligence and exertion, and the utmost (al-ghayah) is the end.
He means: the purity of knowledge guides its bearer to the intended goal through diligence and exertion. Many of the travelers, indeed most of them, travel by their striving and diligence, unaware of the intended goal.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 45–47 (part 2 of 3):

I will give you a very good example of this. A group of people came from distant lands, bearing the signs of blessing and radiance, fine clothing, and a wondrous appearance. People marveled at them and asked them about their condition. They said: "Our land is among the finest of lands, the most complete in every kind of blessing, the most spacious, the most abundant in water, the purest in air, the richest in fruit, and the most moderate in climate. Its people are likewise the most beautiful of people in form and skin. Yet its king cannot be described in beauty, perfection, goodness, knowledge, forbearance, generosity, mercy toward his subjects, and nearness to them. He possesses awe and dominion over all the kings of the regions, so none of them dares to resist or wage war against him. The people of his land are safe from their enemy; fear does not reach their courtyard. Yet he has times when he appears to his subjects, makes it easy for them to enter upon him, and lifts the veil between him and them. When their eyes fall upon him, all the blessings they are in vanish and are effaced from their sight, so that they turn to nothing of them. When he turns to one of them, all the people of the kingdom turn to him with honor and reverence. We are his messengers to the people of the lands, calling them to his presence, and these are his letters to the people. With us is the testimony that removes ill opinion of us and repels the accusation that we lie about him."

When the people heard this and witnessed the condition of the messengers, they divided into groups.

A first group said: "We will not leave our homelands, nor depart from our abodes, nor bear the hardship of a long journey, nor abandon the life, dwellings, and separation from our fathers, sons, and brothers that we are accustomed to, for a matter promised to us in other than this land. We cannot obtain what we have here except after toil and hardship. How then can we move away from it?"

This group saw leaving their homelands and lands as like the soul's separation from its body, for the soul, because of its intense attachment to the body, finds separation from it the most hateful thing, even if it were to depart to lasting bliss.

This group was overcome by the call of the senses and nature over the call of intellect and right guidance.

The second group: when they saw the condition of the messengers, the joy and goodly state they were in, and knew their truthfulness, they prepared to set out for the king's land. They began the journey. Their families, companions, and kinsmen among those who stayed behind opposed them, and the attachment they had to their dwellings, houses, and gardens opposed them. So they began to put one foot forward and draw back the other. When they remembered the goodness of the king's land and the consolation of life there, they advanced toward it. When what they were accustomed to and used to of the shade of their land and its life, and the company of their people and companions, opposed them, they held back from the journey and turned toward them. So they were always between the two callers and the two pullers, until one of them prevailed and grew stronger over the other, and then they went to it.

The third group: they mounted the backs of their resolutions and saw that the king's land was more deserving of them. They resolved themselves upon reaching it, and the blame of the blamers did not turn them back. Yet in their journey there was slowness, in proportion to the weakness of what had been revealed to them of the conditions of that land and of the king's state.

The fourth group: they strove diligently in the journey and persevered in it, traveling at a swift pace. Of them it is said:

"A caravan that traveled while the night let down its curtains, over every dust-covered, dark-faced one,
They drove on resolutions whose lands were lost between them, so their night-journey became on the backs of resolutions,
The stars of the night show them what they seek, over the shoulder of Sirius and the head of the Nпа'im."

Their aspirations are directed toward the journey, and their powers are devoted to it, without turning aside from the greatest goal and the supreme end.

The fifth group: they set themselves to earnest striving in the journey. Their aspiration is attached to the end, so in their journey they keep their gaze fixed on the goal of the journey. It is as if they see it from afar, and it calls them to itself and to its land. They act upon this witness that stands in their hearts.

Each one's work is according to the measure of his witness. Whoever witnesses the goal of the work in his knowledge, his sincerity, his excellence, and his exertion in it are more complete than one who has not witnessed it nor kept it in view, and he does not feel the touch of fatigue and weariness that the absent one feels, and existence itself bears witness to this. Whoever works a work for a king in his presence, while he sees him, is not in the state of one who works in his absence and distance from him, and is not certain of reaching him.

His saying "and it perfects the aspiration of the seeker" means that the purity of this knowledge perfects his aspiration for him. When the aspiration is sound, it rises and ascends. Its falling and baseness come from its illness and sickness; otherwise it is like fire, which seeks to rise and ascend unless it is prevented.

The highest aspirations: an aspiration connected to the Real, glorified is He, in seeking and intention, and which brings creation to Him by invitation and counsel. This is the aspiration of the messengers and their followers. Its soundness is by distinguishing it from the division of its quest, the division of its object, and the division of its path. Rather, its object is united in sincerity, its seeking in truthfulness, and its path in following the guide that Allah has set up as a guide, not one that a person has set up as a guide for himself.

By Allah, the aspirations! How wondrous is their affair and how great their difference. There is an aspiration attached to the One above the Throne, and an aspiration hovering around filth and the latrine. The common people say: "The worth of every man is what he does well." The elite say: "The worth of a man is what he seeks." The elite of the elite say: "A man's aspiration is toward what he seeks."

If you want to know the ranks of aspirations, look at the aspiration of Rabi'ah ibn Ka'b al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "Ask of me," and he said: "I ask you for your companionship in Paradise." Others asked him for what would fill his stomach or cover his skin.

And look at the aspiration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the keys to the treasures of the earth were offered to him, and he refused them. It is known that had he taken them he would have spent them in obedience to his Lord, the Exalted. Yet that lofty aspiration refused to attach to anything from them other than Allah and what He loves. He was offered to exercise dominion with kingship, and he refused it, and chose to act in pure servitude. There is no god but Allah, the Creator of this aspiration, the Creator of the soul that bears it, and the Creator of aspirations that do not exceed the aspirations of the most base of animals.

[Section: The second degree is purity of state, by which the evidences of verification are witnessed]

He said: The second degree is purity of state, by which the evidences of verification are witnessed, by which the sweetness of intimate conversation is tasted, and by which the cosmos is forgotten.

This degree is higher than what precedes it because it is an aspiration of state. State is the fruit of knowledge, and no state is pure except by the purity of the knowledge that yields it. In proportion to the admixture of knowledge is the admixture of state. When the state is pure, the servant, by his purity, witnesses the traces of realities; these are the evidences in himself and in others, upon himself and upon others. He finds the sweetness of intimate conversation. When he is firmly established in this degree, he forgets the cosmos and what is in it of created things.

This degree is specific to the purity of state, just as the first was specific to the purity of knowledge.

State is the conforming and dyeing of the heart by the rulings of the incoming experiences in their variety, and state calls its bearer to the station from which the incoming experience came, just as the fragrance of a good garden calls one to enter it and dwell in it. If the incoming experience comes from a sound presence, which is the presence of the Divine Reality and not the imagined mental reality, the wayfarer, by his purity, witnesses evidences of verification, and these are its signs. Verification is the rule of reality and the heart's and spirit's being affected by it, and reality is what is connected to the Manifest Real, glorified is He. Allah is the Real. Reality is what is ascribed to Him and connected to Him. Verification is the heart's being affected by the traces of reality. Every real has a reality, and every reality has a verification that arises from witnessing the reality.

His saying "and by which the sweetness of intimate conversation is tasted": intimate conversation (munajah) is a form of mufa'alah from najwa, which is address in the secret and inner being of the servant. The Shaykh mentioned three matters in this degree.

The first: witnessing the evidences of verification.

The second: tasting the sweetness of intimate conversation. When his state is purified from impurities, its sweetness is free from the bitterness of troubles, so he tastes that sweetness in the state of his intimate conversation. If the state were mixed and turbid, he would not find the sweetness of intimate conversation.

The state based on an incoming experience by which the sweetness of intimate conversation is tasted belongs to the presence of the Names and Attributes, according to what the heart encounters of their manifestation and the unveiling of their meanings.

So whoever has the Name the Loving (al-Wadud) manifest to him, for example, and has its meanings unveiled, its subtlety, and its connection to the outward and inward of the servant, the state that arises for him from the presence of this Name is fitting to him.

It becomes a state of occupation with love and longing, and the pleasure of intimate conversation, sweeter and better than which there is none, in proportion to his absorption in witnessing the meaning of this Name and his share of its effect.
