The second: tasting the sweetness of intimate conversation. When his state is purified from impurities, its sweetness is free from the bitterness of troubles, so he tastes that sweetness in the state of his intimate conversation. If the state were mixed and turbid, he would not find the sweetness of intimate conversation.

The state based on an incoming experience by which the sweetness of intimate conversation is tasted belongs to the presence of the Names and Attributes, according to what the heart encounters of their manifestation and the unveiling of their meanings.

So whoever has the Name the Loving (al-Wadud) manifest to him, for example, and has its meanings unveiled, its subtlety, and its connection to the outward and inward of the servant, the state that arises for him from the presence of this Name is fitting to him.

It becomes a state of occupation with love and longing, and the pleasure of intimate conversation, sweeter and better than which there is none, in proportion to his absorption in witnessing the meaning of this Name and his share of its effect.

Al-Wadud, even if it means the one who is loved, as al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "al-Wadud is the Beloved," and the servant's absorption in contemplating the attributes of perfection that call the servant to love the One described by them yields him purity of knowledge of them and purity of state in worshipping according to their requirement: these three matters the Shaykh mentioned, and others.

Likewise, if it is an active participle meaning the one who loves, that contemplation yields him a state suitable to it.

For when he witnesses in his heart a Generous, Bountiful, Munificent, Mighty, Powerful One, to whom everyone is essentially in need, who is essentially independent of all else, and who—despite that—loves His servants, and draws near to them through His goodness to them and His favor upon them, he has from this witnessing a pure state free from impurities.

Likewise all the Names and Attributes. The purity of state is in proportion to the purity of knowledge of them and their freedom from the blood of negation and the dung of anthropomorphism. Knowledge thus emerges from between them as a pure natural disposition, palatable to the knowers, just as milk emerges from between dung and blood as pure milk, palatable to drinkers.

The third matter: his saying "and by which the cosmos is forgotten," meaning the cosmos is forgotten by what predominates over his heart of his occupation with this mentioned state. The cosmos means created things; that is, he occupies himself with the Real and is turned away from creation.

[Section: The third degree is purity of connection]

He said: The third degree is purity of connection. It strips the portion of servitude into the right of lordship, drowns the ends of report in the beginnings of direct vision, and folds the baseness of obligations into the very eternity.

In this expression there is discomfort and poor phrasing, which is remedied by the good state of its speaker, his truthfulness, and his veneration of Allah and His Messenger. But Allah refused that perfection belongs to anyone other than Himself. There is no doubt that between the people of states and the people of established station there is a great difference. Consider the dominance of state over Moses, peace be upon him, when he witnessed the traces of the Divine manifestation upon the mountain: how he fell down thunderstruck! And the one of established station, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, when he was taken on the Night Journey and saw what he saw: he was not struck senseless nor fell down, but his heart and sight remained firm.

What the people of this path mean by connection and arrival is the servant's connection to his Lord and his arrival to Him, not in the sense of the connection of the essence of the servant to the essence of the Lord, as two essences connect one to the other, nor in the sense of one essence joining to the other and clinging to it. Rather, what they mean by connection and arrival is the removal of the self and creation from the path of traveling to Allah. Do not imagine anything other than this, for that is sheer impossibility.

For the wayfarer never ceases traveling to Allah, the Exalted, until he dies. His journey does not end except by death. There is no arrival in this life at which the inner secret is emptied and concluded. Nor is there a sensible connection between the essence of the servant and the essence of the Lord. The first is nullification and atheism; the second is indwelling and unification. The true reality is only the removal of self and creation from the path, for to stand still with them is cutting off, and removing them is connection.

The heretics who hold the doctrine of the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud) say: the servant is among the acts of God, His acts are among His attributes, and His attributes are part of His essence. From this chain they conclude that the servant is part of the essence of the Lord. Exalted is God, far above what they say, to a great height.

The point of error is that the servant is among the created effects (maf'ulat) of the Lord, the Exalted, not among His acts that subsist in His essence. His effects are the traces of His acts. His acts are among His attributes that subsist in His essence. So His Being, glorified is He, necessarily entails His attributes and His acts, while His effects are separate from Him; those are created and originated. The Lord, the Exalted, is the Creator by His essence, His attributes, and His acts.

So beware, then beware, of the ambiguous and equivocal terms that the people of this path have adopted as their technical vocabulary, for they are the root of the trial, and they are the ground where the sincere believer and the heretic meet.

When one who is weak in knowledge and in the knowledge of God, the Exalted, hears the words "union and separation, intimate converse, speaking with Him," and that "there is no existence in reality except the existence of God, and the existence of created beings is imagination and illusion, like the existence of a shadow that subsists by another," he will hear from him what fills the ears of incarnation, fusion, and ecstatic utterances (shathahat).

The knowers among this people used these words and their like, meaning by them correct meanings in themselves. But those who err misunderstood what they intended, and attributed to them heresy and disbelief. They took their ambiguous expressions as a shield and a covering, until one of them said:

"From You there appeared a love, with might, that mingled
between us, and the union You were, You were the one who joined it."

"You appeared to the one whom You left after his annihilation,
and he was without existence, for You were his being."

The ignorant one hears "mingling" and "union," and thinks that He, glorified is He, is the very being of the servant. He doubts not that this is the ultimate realization and the end of the path. Now let us return to the explanation of his words.

His saying: "He includes the portion of servanthood within the right of lordship."

The correct meaning that this statement can bear is that whoever has firmly established in his heart the witnessing of the Names and Attributes, and whose knowledge and state have become pure, his whole deed, and its multiples, and multiples of multiples, is subsumed within the right of his Lord, the Exalted. He sees it, beside the right of his Lord, as less than a mustard seed in comparison to the mountains of this world. So there falls from his heart the claim of his own share of reward for it, because of his contempt for it, its insignificance in his sight, and its smallness in his eyes.

Imam Ahmad said: Hashim ibn al-Qasim narrated to us: Salih narrated to us, from Abu Imran al-Jawni, from Abu al-Jild, that God, the Exalted, revealed to Dawud: "O Dawud, warn My truthful servants. Let them not be pleased with themselves, nor rely upon their deeds. For there is none of My servants whom I set up for reckoning and establish My justice over, except that I punish him, not because I have wronged him. And give good news to My sinning servants: that no sin is too great for Me to forgive and overlook."

And Imam Ahmad said: Sayyar narrated to us: Ja'far narrated to us: Thabit al-Bunani narrated to us, saying: A man worshipped for seventy years, and he used to say in his supplication: "My Lord, reward me for my deed." Then he died and was admitted into Paradise, and he remained there for seventy years. When his time was complete, it was said to him: "Go out, for you have received your deed in full." He reflected on what in the world he had been most confident of in himself, and found nothing he was more confident of than the supplication to God and turning to Him. So he began to say in his supplication: "My Lord, I heard You, while I was in the world, saying: You pardon the stumbles. So pardon my stumble today." And he was left in Paradise.

And Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: Hashim narrated to us: Salih narrated to us, from Abu Imran al-Jawni, from Abu al-Jild, who said: Musa said: "My God, how can I thank You, when the smallest blessing You placed with me from Your blessings is not repaid by all my deeds?" God, the Exalted, revealed to him: "O Musa, now you have thanked Me."

This is the correct meaning of the inclusion of the portion of servanthood within the right of lordship.

It also has another correct interpretation: that the essence of the servant, his attributes, his acts, his powers, and his movements are all effects made by the Lord, owned by Him. The servant possesses none of them; rather, they are purely God's possession. He is the owner of them, and the one who bestows His blessing upon His servant by giving them to him. So the wealth is His wealth, the servant is His servant, and the service is due to Him by right of lordship. And it is from God's grace upon him. So all grace belongs to God, is from God, and is by God.

His saying: "He knows the ends of the report in the beginnings of direct vision." The "report" (al-khabar) is the object of the unseen (al-ghayb). The "direct vision" (al-ʿiyan) is the object of the witnessed (al-shahadah). It is the perception by the eye of insight of the truth of the report and the establishment of what it reports.

By "the beginnings of direct vision" he means the first stages of true unveiling (al-kashf al-haqiqi), through which one enters the station of annihilation (fana'). His intention is that the one who witnesses sees with his heart what the Truthful One has reported, as if by direct sight. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [Saba: 6], and He said: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19]. So He is saying: Is one who sees with the eye of his heart that what God has sent down to His Messenger is the truth like one who is blind and does not perceive this? And the Prophet (ﷺ) said, regarding the station of excellence (ihsan): "That you worship God as if you see Him." There is no doubt that affirming the report and certainty in it strengthens the heart, until the unseen becomes like the seen with the eye. So the possessor of this station is as if he sees his Lord, glorified is He, above His heavens, on His Throne, overlooking His servants, watching them, hearing their speech, and seeing their outward and inward states.

It is as if he hears Him speaking through revelation, speaking to His servant Jibril, commanding and forbidding him as He wills, and directing the affairs of the kingdom, with His angels ascending to Him with the command and descending from Him with it.

It is as if he sees Him, as He is pleased and angry, loves and hates, gives and withholds, laughs and rejoices, praises His friends among His angels, and condemns His enemies.

It is as if he sees Him and sees His two noble hands, one of which holds the seven heavens and the other the seven earths. And He folds the seven heavens with His right hand, as a scroll is folded over the lines of a book.

It is as if he sees Him, as He comes to judge between His servants. The earth shines with His light.

And He calls out, while seated upon His Throne, with a voice heard by the far as it is heard by the near: "By My might and My majesty: no wrongdoer's injustice shall transcend Me today."

And it is as if he hears His call to Adam: "O Adam, rise and send forth the group for the Fire," by His permission now; and likewise His call to the people of the place of standing: ﴿What did you answer the messengers?﴾ [al-Qasas: 65] "And what were you worshipping?"

In sum: he sees with his heart a Lord made known by the Messengers, as the Books made Him known, and a religion to which the Messengers called, and realities that the Messengers reported. The witness of this stands in his heart just as the witness of what the mass-transmitted reports say about cities and events stands, even if he has not seen them. So his faith flows in the way of direct vision, while the faith of others is nothing but the imitation of the blind.

His saying: "And he folds the baseness of obligations." I wish the Shaykh had expressed this word with something else. By God, it is more repugnant than a thorn in the eye and a bone stuck in the throat. Obligations are far too exalted to be described as base, or to be touched by baseness. Rather they are the coolness of the eye, the joy of the heart, and the life of the soul. The obligation was issued by the Wise, the Praiseworthy. So they are the most noble thing that reaches the servant from his Lord, and the reward for them is the most noble that God gives to the servant.

Yes, had he said "he folds the burden of obligations and lightens their weight, and the like," perhaps that would have been better. And were it not for his station in faith, knowledge, and standing firm in the commands, we would have thought ill of him because of it.

There are two possible ways to turn his words:

The first: that the purity mentioned in this degree, when the intermediaries and causes are folded into his judgment, and the portion of servanthood is included within the right of lordship, then within it the vision of worship as an obligation is also folded. For seeing it as an obligation is a baseness on the part of the seer, because he sees it through the lens of his own self-regard and his own standing in it, and not through the lens of reality. For he has not reached the station of "By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he strikes, by Me he walks." Had he reached that, he would see it through the lens of reality, and there would be no baseness in it at all there.

For his gaze has passed beyond his own standing in it, to its standing by the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum), by whom everything subsists.

So it has two aspects:

One: it is base in itself, and this is the aspect of its subsistence in the servant and its proceeding from him.

The other: it is noble through Him, and this is the aspect of its being by the Lord, the Exalted, and of His priority, as command, as creation, and as aid. So the purity folds it from that particular aspect alone.

The second meaning his words may bear: that the purity he mentions is witnessed by the eye of the Pre-Eternal (al-Azal), and by the precedence of the Lord, the Exalted, and His priority over everything. In this witnessing, the deeds he has done are folded up, and he sees them as extremely base compared to the eye of the Pre-Eternal. So it is as if he said: his deeds are folded, and become, in relation to this eye, extremely base, not worth mentioning. Indeed, in the eye of the Pre-Eternal they are scattered dust, with no real substance.

For the time that is the container of obligation fades away greatly in relation to the Pre-Eternal. It is a base and worthless time, so much that it seems to have no substance. It has no proportion at all to the Pre-Eternal and the Everlasting, in the measure of the deeds done within it. And they are small in comparison to the whole of that time, which is itself extremely small, compared to the whole of time, which is itself extremely small, compared to the very eye of the Pre-Eternal.

This is the closest that his words can be taken to mean, despite their unease. Poor expression has befallen them. It seems he applied the word "baseness" to them because of their scarcity and lightness in relation to the greatness of the One who imposes them, glorified is He, and what He deserves. And God, glorified is He, knows best.

Consider His words, "Gardens of Eden, their gates thrown open for them" (38:50). How do you find a wonderful meaning beneath it?

It means that when the people of Paradise enter it, its gates are not locked upon them; they remain open just as they are. As for the Fire, when its people enter it, its gates are locked upon them, as Allah, the Exalted, says: "Over them will be a closed vault" (90:20).

That is, sealed shut and closed. From this comes the word "al-bab" (gate) and "wasad" (a closing). It is "mu'sadah" (sealed) with outstretched pillars, the pillars holding the doors shut from behind them, like the great stone placed behind a door.

Muqatil said: "Its gates are sealed over them, so no door is opened for them and no sorrow goes out from it, and no other spirit enters it, forever."

Also, in the opening of the gates for them there is an indication of their freedom of movement, their going and coming, their settling in Paradise wherever they wish, the angels entering upon them at all times with gifts and kindnesses from their Lord, and whatever gladdens them entering upon them at all times.

Also, it indicates that it is an abode of security, where they have no need to lock doors, as they needed to do in this world.

The grammarians differed concerning the pronoun returning from the adjective to the noun it describes in this clause.

The Kufans said: the implied sense is "opened for them, its gates." The Arabs interchange the definite article "al" and the possessive construction, saying "marartu bi-rajulin hasan al-ayn," meaning "hasan aynuh" (a man whose eye is good). From this is His saying, "Indeed, Hell is the refuge" (79:39), meaning "its refuge."

Some of the Basrans said: the implied sense is "opened for them, the gates in it." The pronoun and what is attached to it were omitted.

He said: this estimate is better in Arabic than making the "al" a substitute for the "ha" and "alif." This is because the meaning of "al" has nothing in common with the meaning of the pronoun, since the pronoun is a noun, while "al" was introduced for definiteness. A letter is not substituted for a noun nor does it stand in for it.

They said: Also, if "al" were a substitute for the pronoun, then "mufattahah" would have to have a pronoun referring to "gardens," and the meaning would be "opened, it (they)," then "the gates" would be a substitute for it. If that were the case, "the gates" would have to be in the accusative, because "mufattahah" already has a subject pronoun in the nominative, and it is not permissible for another noun to be in the nominative by it, since two subjects cannot both be nominative for one verb.

Since "al-abwab" is in the nominative, this shows that "mufattahah" is a circumstantial (hal) qualifier of a pronoun, and "al-abwab" is nominative by it. When there is a pronoun in the descriptive word, the second must be in the accusative, as you say "marartu bi-rajulin hasan al-wajh." If you made "al-wajh" nominative and gave "hasan" tanwin, it would not be permissible. So "al" is only for definiteness, and there must be a pronoun returning to the described noun, which is "Gardens of Eden," and there is no pronoun in the wording. It is therefore omitted, its estimate being: "the gates of it."

In my view, this does not invalidate the Kufans' position. They did not mean by substitution anything more than that "al" is a replacement and compensation for the pronoun that stands in for it. The consensus of the Arabs on their saying "hasan al-wajh" and "hasan wajhuh" (good of face) is evidence for this.

They have said that tanwin is a substitute for "al," meaning that the two do not combine, and likewise the genitive attached is a substitute for tanwin, and tanwin a substitute for the construct, in the sense of interchange and alternation. By their saying "this is a substitute for that," they do not mean that the meaning of the substitute is the meaning of what it replaces, but that each may have a meaning the other lacks.

So the Kufans meant that "al" in "al-abwab" stands in for the pronoun, or it is said "abwabuha" (its gates), and this is correct. The intended point is the linking of the qualifier with the qualified by something that makes it belong to it, not standing independently. Since the pronoun returns to the described noun, the appearance of independence is negated, and likewise the definite article: each of the pronoun and the "al" specifies its counterpart, one specifying what it explains and the other specifying what it is attached to. They have said, regarding "Zayd, what an excellent man," that "al" has replaced the pronoun. And Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari parsed this verse in a manner that was objected to. He said: "Gardens of Eden" is definite by His saying, "Gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen" (19:61).

It is in the accusative as an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to "husn ma'ab" (a good return), and "mufattahah" is a circumstantial qualifier, its governing element being the meaning of the verb within "al-muttaqin." In "mufattahah" is a pronoun referring to the gardens, and "al-abwab" is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, its estimate being: "opened, they are the gates," like the saying "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," which is a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). This is his parsing.

He was objected to: that "Gardens of Eden" contains nothing requiring its definiteness. As for His saying "which the Most Merciful promised," it is a substitute, not a qualifier. And that "Gardens of Eden" cannot easily be an explanatory apposition to "husn ma'ab" in his statement, because the definite following the indefinite as explanatory apposition is something no one holds.

The sayers are two: one holds that it occurs only with definites, as the Basrans say; the other holds that it occurs with definites and indefinites under the condition of agreement, as the Kufans and Abu Ali al-Farisi say.

As for his statement that the pronoun in "mufattahah" refers to the gardens, the apparent meaning is contrary to it, since "al-abwab" is nominative by it and there is no pronoun in it.

As for his statement that "al-abwab" is a substitute of inclusion, he and others have stated explicitly that a substitute of inclusion must have a pronoun. Others dispute this, but the pronoun may be pronounced or implied. Here it is not pronounced, so an estimate is necessary: "the gates of it." If the estimate is "opened for them, they are the gates of it," then it involves more omission, and reducing omission is better.

(Section)

In the Two Sahihs, from the narration of Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"In Paradise there are eight gates, one of which is called ar-Rayyan, which only those who fast will enter."

In the Two Sahihs, from the narration of az-Zuhri, from Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever spends two of anything in the way of Allah will be called from the gates of Paradise: 'O servant of Allah, this is good.' Whoever is among the people of prayer will be called from the gate of prayer; whoever is among the people of jihad will be called from the gate of jihad; whoever is among the people of charity will be called from the gate of charity; and whoever is among the people of fasting will be called from the gate of ar-Rayyan." Abu Bakr said: "May my father and mother be ransomed for you, O Messenger of Allah! There is no need for anyone called from those gates, so will anyone be called from all of them?" He said: "Yes, and I hope you will be among them."

In Sahih Muslim, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"None of you performs wudu, perfecting or completing the ablution, then says: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger,' except that the eight gates of Paradise will be opened for him, and he may enter by whichever he wishes."

At-Tirmidhi added after the testimony: "O Allah, make me among those who repent, and make me among those who purify themselves." Abu Dawud and Imam Ahmad added: "Then he raised his gaze to the sky and said..."

In Imam Ahmad, from the narration of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever performs wudu and perfects it, then says three times: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger,' the eight gates of Paradise will be opened for him, and he may enter by whichever he wishes."

From Utba ibn Abd Allah as-Sulami, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say:

"No Muslim who loses three children who have not reached puberty will fail to be met by them at the eight gates of Paradise; he may enter by whichever he wishes."

Narrated by Ibn Majah and Abdullah ibn Ahmad, from Ibn Numayr, from Ishaq ibn Sulayman, from Jarir ibn Uthman, from Shurahbil ibn Shafa, from Utba.

(Section: on the width of its gates)

From Abu Hurayra, who said: A bowl of thareed with meat was placed before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He took the foreleg, which was his favourite part of the sheep, and bit off a mouthful, and said: "I am the chief of mankind on the Day of Resurrection." Then he bit another and said: "I am the chief of mankind on the Day of Resurrection." When he saw that his companions did not ask him, he said: "Will you not say, 'How?'" They said: "How, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The people will stand before the Lord of the worlds; the Caller will make them hear, and the sight will penetrate them." Then he related the hadith of intercession at length, and at its end he said: "I will go and come under the Throne, and fall down prostrate to my Lord. The Lord of the worlds will raise me to a station no one before me has been raised to, and none after me will be raised to. I will say: 'O Lord, my nation, my nation!' He will say: 'O Muhammad, admit from your nation those who have no reckoning from the right-hand gate, and they will share with the people in the other gates.' By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, what lies between the two leaves of the gates of Paradise is like what lies between Makkah and Hajar, or Hajar and Makkah."

In another wording: "like what lies between Makkah and Hajar," or "as between Makkah and Busra."

Agreed upon as authentic.

In a wording outside the Sahih, with its chain: "What lies between the two posts of the gate is like what lies between Makkah and Hajar."

From Khalid ibn Umayr al-Adawi, who said: Utba ibn Ghazwan addressed us, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "To proceed: the world has announced its departure and turned its back, and nothing of it remains but a remnant like the dregs of a vessel that its owner drinks. You are moving from it to an abode that has no end, so depart with the best of what is in your presence. It has been mentioned to us that between two leaves of the gates of Paradise is a distance of forty years, and a day will certainly come upon it when it is crowded with people." This is a mawquf (companion's) report, while the preceding is marfu' (traced to the Prophet). If it was the Prophet (ﷺ) who related this, then this is what lies between one of its gates, perhaps the greatest gate. If the one relating it was someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ), it does not take precedence over the hadith of Abu Hurayra mentioned earlier.

However, Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad, by way of Hammad ibn Salama al-Jurayri, from Hakim ibn Muawiya, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will complete seventy nations, you being the last and the most honoured of them before Allah, and what lies between two leaves of the gates of Paradise is a distance of forty years, and a day will certainly come upon it when it is crowded."

Ibn Abi Dawud also narrated it: Ishaq ibn Shahin informed us, Khalid informed us, from al-Jurayri, from Hakim ibn Muawiya, from his father, traced to the Prophet: "Between every two leaves of the gates of Paradise is a distance of seven years."

In the Musnad of Abd ibn Humayd, we have it: al-Hasan ibn Musa informed us, Ibn Lahi'a informed us, Darraj Abu as-Samh informed us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "There are no two leaves in Paradise whose distance is forty years."

The hadith of Abu Hurayra is more authentic, and these versions are weak, and Allah knows best.

Abu ash-Shaykh narrated: Ja'far ibn Ahmad ibn Faris informed us, Ya'qub ibn Humayd informed us, Ma'n informed us, Khalid ibn Abi Bakr informed us, from Salim ibn Abd Allah, from his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The gate through which the people of Paradise enter is the distance of a well-trained rider three times over, and they will press upon it until their shoulders almost fall away." Abu Nu'aym narrated it from him. This agrees with the agreed-upon hadith: "What lies between the two leaves is as between Makkah and Busra," since the well-trained rider at the utmost of skill, on a swift riding camel that never tires by night or by day, covers this distance in this amount of time or close to it.

As for the hadith of Hakim ibn Muawiya, its narrators are confused: Hammad ibn Salama reported from al-Jurayri the figure of forty years, while Khalid reported from him the figure of seven years. The marfu' hadith of Abu Sa'id, with its figure of forty years, through Darraj from Abu al-Haytham, is also problematic: Imam Ahmad said the reports of Darraj are unknown (munkar), Abu Hatim al-Razi said he is weak, and al-Nasa'i said he is not strong. (Section: on the description of its gates and that they have rings)

Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated from Khulayd, from al-Hasan, regarding "their gates thrown open for them," that he said: "Gates which can be seen." He also reported from Khulayd, from Qatada, that he said: "Gates whose outside is seen from the inside and whose inside is seen from the outside; they speak and are spoken to, and understand what is said to them: 'Open!' 'Close!'"

Abu ash-Shaykh said: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Qaysi informed us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawwari informed us, Abd Allah ibn Ghiyath informed us, from al-Fazari, who said: Every believer in Paradise has four gates. One gate through which his visiting angels enter; one gate through which his wives of the dark-eyed houris enter; one locked gate between him and the people of the Fire, which he opens whenever he wishes to look at them, so that the blessing upon him may be magnified; and one gate between him and the Abode of Peace, through which he enters upon his Lord whenever he wishes.

Suhayl ibn Abi Salih narrated from Ziyad al-Namari, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will be the first to take hold of the ring of the gate of Paradise, and I say this without boasting."

In the long hadith of intercession, from the narration of Ibn Uyayna, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will take hold of the ring of the gate of Paradise and rattle it."

This is explicit that it is a tangible ring that moves and rattles.

Suhayl narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I will take hold of the ring of the gate of Paradise, and it will be opened for me." It is also related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah, the King, the Manifest Truth' one hundred times every day, he will have security from poverty and from the loneliness of the grave, will attract wealth by it, and will knock at the gate of Paradise by it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 52–53:

The exegetes are all agreed that the meaning is: they restrict their gaze to their husbands, so they do not look longingly toward anyone else. It was also said: they restrict the gaze of all their husbands, so that their beauty and loveliness do not allow them to look toward anyone other than them. This is sound in meaning. As for the wording, qasirat (قاصِرات, "restricting") is a descriptive adjective construction (idafah) attached to the agent, referring to those with beautiful faces; its original form is qasir tarfuhunna, meaning that their gaze is not roving, and it is intransitive (la ratih) rather than transitive (muta'addi).

Adam said: Warqa' narrated to us from Abu Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Restricting their gaze﴾.

He said: He says, "restricting their gaze to their husbands, so they do not desire anyone other than their husbands." Adam also said: Al-Mubarak ibn Fadalah narrated to us from al-Hasan, who said: "They restricted their gaze to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else. By Allah, they are neither ostentatious nor eager to be seen." Mansur said, from Mujahid: "They restricted their eyes, their hearts, and their selves to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else." In the tafsir of Sa'id, from Qatadah, he said: "And they restricted their gazes to their husbands, so they do not turn toward anyone else."

As for al-atrab (الأتراب), it is the plural of atrab (ترب), which is the peer of a person (lidhdhat al-insan).

Abu Ubaydah said, and Abu Ishaq (said): their ages are equal, one age. Ibn Abbas and the rest of the exegetes said: "Equal in one age, one birth, and aged thirty-three years."

Mujahid said: atrab means "similar."

Ishaq said: "They are in the prime of youth and beauty." The age of a person and his contemporary is called turbah (تربه) because he touched the dust of the earth at the same time as him. The meaning, according to the best reading, is by the equality of their ages: there are no elderly women among them whose beauty has passed, nor young girls who cannot bear intercourse, unlike the males, among whom are the wildan, who are the servants.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 38, verses 59–61:**

Their saying: ﴿You brought it upon us, so wretched is the abode﴾ means: you set it as a precedent (sannatumūhu) for us and legislated it (sharaʿtumūhu) for us.

Their saying: ﴿Welcome not to them! Indeed, they will burn in the Fire﴾ means: they entered it just as we entered it, and they suffer its punishment just as we suffer it.

The followers answered them and said: ﴿Rather, it is you! Welcome not to you! You brought it upon us﴾.

There are two opinions regarding the pronoun (ḍamīr):

The first is that it refers to disbelief and denial, and to the rejection of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the substitution of other than him for him. The meaning is: you adorned disbelief for us, called us to it, and made it appealing to us. It was said, according to this view, that it is the saying of the later nations to the earlier ones. The meaning according to this view is: you legislated for us the denial of the messengers, the rejection of what they brought, and association with Allah, the Exalted, and you began it and went before us to it, so you entered the Fire before us. ﴿So wretched is the abode﴾, that is, wretched is the place of settlement and dwelling.

The second opinion is that the pronoun in His saying ﴿You brought it upon us﴾ refers to the punishment and the burning of the Fire. The two opinions are mutually consistent, and both are true.

As for those who say: ﴿Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase him in punishment, double, in the Fire﴾,

it is possible that the followers invoked this against their leaders, chiefs and imams, because they are the ones who drove them to it and called them to it.

It is also possible that all the people of the Fire asked their Lord to double the punishment of those who established for them association with Allah and denial of the messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, and they are the devils.

If it is said: how does (mā) come to be used for one who has intellect, as in His saying: ﴿for that which I created with My two hands﴾, ﴿and the sky and He who built it﴾, ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾,

and similar examples?

It is said: in all of this, (mā) remains on its original basis of indefiniteness and of applying to the general class. What (mā) intends is what (man) intends, namely specification of the rational being and restriction rather than generality. Whoever understands the true meaning of speech and has a sense for it will recognize this and find it clear.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My hands?﴾ this is a statement given in the context of rebuke and reproach to Iblis for refusing to prostrate. This rebuke and reproach would not have been deserved merely because the prostration was owed to one who has intellect; rather it was for the disobedience and for arrogance toward what He had not created, since arrogance is not fitting for one created toward his own kind; arrogance belongs to the Creator alone. It is as if He, glorified is He, were saying: Why did you disobey Me and act arrogantly toward what you did not create, while I created it, honored it, and commanded you to prostrate to it?

This is the place for (mā), because its meaning is more far-reaching and its wording more general; it is more forceful in argument and cuts off excuse and doubt.

Had He said: "What prevented you from prostrating to the one whom I created?" it would have been a plain question free of rebuke and reproach, and it would have suggested that prostration was owed to him because he has intellect, and perhaps because he exists in his own essence and identity. That is not the intent. The intent is to rebuke him and reprove him for leaving prostration to what God created and commanded him to prostrate to. For this reason He turned away from the proper name Adam, even though it is more specific, and used the relative pronoun, which indicates the aspect of honor that requires prostration to him, namely that He created him with His hands.

If you were to put the word (man) in place of (mā), you would not see this meaning mentioned in the relative clause, nor that it was used to lead to the mention of the clause.

So reflect on this: there is then no meaning in specifying by mention, for if specification were intended, the proper name would have been more fitting and more appropriate.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And the sky and what built it﴾, because an oath is a magnification of the one sworn by, and his deserving of magnification is from the aspect of (mā): it manifests this great creation which is the sky, and from the aspect that He made it even and adorned it with His wisdom, so He deserves magnification and His power is established. Had He said "and He who built it," there would be no indication in the wording of His deserving to be sworn by from the aspect that He was capable of building it, and the meaning would have been confined to His essence and self, without alluding to His acts that show His greatness, that announce His wisdom, and that declare His deserving of magnification from His creation.

Likewise the saying: "Glory be to what the thunder glorifies with its praise," because thunder is a loud sound from a great body, and that which is glorified by it is certainly greater; so its deserving of glorification is from the aspect that the great beings of His creation deserve it, not from the aspect that it knows. Do not say "who" (ya'qil) in this context.

When you reflect on what we have mentioned, the deficiency of those who say that (mā) with the verb in all of this is other than the first use, being in the sense of a verbal noun, becomes clear to you. Such a person has not measured the meaning by its due measure: he has not succeeded in the science of grammar, nor been granted understanding of tafsir; he followed the surface and missed the joint, circled around the matter but did not reach the watering place.

In (al-Sawa'iq al-Mursala) he said:

The word "yad" (hand) occurs in the Qur'an in three forms: singular, dual, and plural.

The singular: as in His saying: ﴿in whose hand is the dominion﴾; the dual: as in His saying: ﴿I created with My two hands﴾; and the plural: as in His saying: ﴿what Our hands have done﴾.

Where "hand" is mentioned in the dual, He attributes the act to Himself with the singular pronoun, and makes the verb transitive to the two hands with the preposition (bi), saying: ﴿I created with My two hands﴾.

Where He mentions it in the plural, He attributes the act to the hands and does not make the verb transitive with (bi).

These are three differences. So "I created with My two hands" cannot bear the figurative meaning that ﴿what Our hands have done﴾ can bear, for everyone understands from His saying ﴿what Our hands have done﴾ what they understand from "we did" and "we created," just as they understand it from His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾.

As for His saying ﴿I created with My two hands﴾: had the meaning been merely the act, there would be no point in mentioning the hand after attributing the act to the agent. How much more so when the preposition (bi) has been placed upon it, and even more so when it is in the dual?

The secret of the difference is that an act may be attributed to the hand of the one who has a hand, and what is meant is the attribution to him, as in His saying ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾ and ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾.

But when the act is attributed to Him and then made transitive by (bi) to the hand, singular or dual, it is something His hand actually did.

For this reason, Abdullah ibn Umar said: "God did not create with His hand except three things: He created Adam with His hand, He planted the Garden of Firdaws with His hand, and He wrote the Torah with His hand." Had the hand meant power, it would not have had any special feature in this, nor would Adam have had any virtue over everything else created by power.

The Prophet ﷺ informed that "the people of the gathering will come to him on the Day of Resurrection and say: O Adam, you are the father of mankind, God created you with His hand."

Likewise Adam said to Musa in his argument with him: "God chose you with His speech and wrote the tablets for you with His hand."

In another wording: "He wrote the Torah for you with His hand," and this is among the most authentic hadiths. Likewise the well-known hadith: "The angels said: O Lord, You created the children of Adam, who eat, drink, marry and ride, so make the world for them and the Hereafter for us. Since the Muslims understood that His saying ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My hands?﴾ entails a special distinction and preference for him, being created with two hands, over the one he was commanded to prostrate to, and since the people of the gathering understood it and counted it among his special qualities, then to equate it with His saying ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, of what Our hands have done, cattle?﴾ would be sheer error.

God, exalted is He, said: I will not make the righteous of the offspring of those whom I created with My hand and into whom I breathed of My spirit like one to whom I said 'Be,' and he was."

This specification was understood only from His saying "created with My hands." Had it been like His saying "of what Our hands have done," he and the cattle would have been equal in that. Since the Muslims understood that His saying ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My hands?﴾ entails a special distinction and preference for him, being created with two hands, over the one he was commanded to prostrate to, and since the people of the gathering understood it and counted it among his special qualities, then to equate it with His saying ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, of what Our hands have done, cattle?﴾ would be sheer error.

When the enemy of Allah knew that Allah, the Exalted, would not give him power over the people of tawhid (monotheism) and sincerity, he said: ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except among them Your sincere servants."﴾

So the enemy of Allah knew that whoever holds fast to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sincerely devotes himself to Him, and relies upon Him, he cannot be led astray or misguided by Satan. Rather, he (Satan) has authority only over those who take him as a protector and associate others with Allah. Those are his subjects, and he is their guardian, their ruler, and the one they follow.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 38, verse 86:

The Prophet (ﷺ) censured those who go to extremes in religion (al-mutanaṭṭi'ūn), and informed of their ruin when he said:

"Woe to the extremists! Woe to the extremists! Woe to the extremists!"

Ibn Abi Shaybah said: Abu Usamah narrated to us from Mis'ar, who said: "A book was brought out to Ma'n ibn Abd al-Rahman, and he swore by Allah that it was his father's handwriting, and in it was: Abd Allah said: By Allah, other than Whom there is no god, I have not seen anyone more severe against the extremists than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor have I seen anyone after him more fearful for them than Abu Bakr. And I think that Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was the most fearful of them among the people of the earth."

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to dislike those who over-deepen (al-mut'ammiqūn), to the extent that when he continued fasting without breaking it (al-wiṣāl) with them and saw the crescent, he said: "If the crescent had not appeared, I would have continued a continuous fast with you, leaving those who over-deepen in their over-deepening, as one who makes them an example."

The Companions were the least of the Ummah in artificiality (takalluf), following the example of their Prophet (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it, and I am not of those who affect (what is not theirs).﴾ [Sad: 86]

ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Whoever among you would follow a path, let him follow those who have passed away, for the living is not safe from temptation. Those were the Companions of Muhammad: the most righteous of this Ummah in heart, the deepest of them in knowledge, and the least of them in artificiality. A people whom Allah chose for the companionship of His Prophet. So recognise their rights, and hold fast to their guidance, for they were upon the straight guidance."

Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We were with Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and I heard him say: We have been forbidden artificiality."

Malik said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the rulers after him established sunnahs; adhering to them is confirmation of the Book of Allah, the exercise of obedience to Allah, and strength in the religion of Allah. It is not for anyone to change or alter them, nor to consider what opposes them. Whoever follows them is guided, whoever seeks victory through them is victorious, and whoever opposes them and follows other than the way of the believers, Allah will leave him to what he has chosen and cast him into Hell, and evil is the destination."

Malik said: It reached me that Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say:

"The sunnahs have been established for you, the obligations have been prescribed for you, and you have been left upon the clear path, unless you turn the people to the right and to the left."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"This knowledge will be carried by the trustworthy of every generation, who will remove from it the distortion of the extremists, the false claims of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretation of the ignorant."

So he informed that the extremists distort what he brought, the falsifiers claim by their falsehood other than what it was upon, and the ignorant interpret it other than its intended meaning.

The corruption of Islam comes from these three groups.

Were it not that Allah the Exalted raises up for His religion those who remove this from it, there would befall it what befell the religions of the prophets before him from such people.
